t: Prime In Diagonal — Diagonal Scan + Primality
o: Collect every value nums[i][i] and nums[i][n-1-i], return the largest prime among them, or 0. Values are at most 4·10^6 and the matrix is at most 300×300, so at most ~600 candidates; trial division up to sqrt(4e6) ≈ 2000 per candidate is plenty fast.
k: Only ~n diagonal cells matter — never scan the whole matrix.
sqrt(4·10^6) = 2000, so per-value trial division is cheap; a sieve is optional.

a.n: Approach 1: Trial division per diagonal value
a.i: Iterate i from 0..n-1, test both diagonal entries for primality by checking divisors up to sqrt(v), and track the maximum prime found.
s: For each i: for v in {nums[i][i], nums[i][n-1-i]}: if v > best and isPrime(v): best = v.
a.t: O(n · sqrt(M)) — n <= 300 candidates, each tested up to sqrt(4e6) = 2000.

a.i: Sieve up to the maximum diagonal value once (≤ 4·10^6), then answer each candidate in O(1). Better when there are many queries or candidates; slightly more memory here.
s: Build a boolean sieve of size maxV+1.
Scan diagonals, tracking the largest sieved-prime value.
a.t: O(M log log M + n) — sieving up to M = max diagonal value dominates.

w: Trial division is the pragmatic choice; pull out the sieve only if asked about many queries. Pitfalls: treating 1 as prime, forgetting the anti-diagonal index n-1-i, and checking candidates in order rather than against the current best (harmless but wasteful). Follow-up: primes on all anti-diagonals of submatrices, or k-th largest diagonal prime.
